title: FTC alleges Amazon illegally made $20 billion by rigging billions of ad auctions
gist: The FTC and 22 state attorneys general sued Amazon alleging it secretly inserted an undisclosed "soft reserve price" into its Sponsored Products, Brands and Display ad auctions starting in 2019, extracting over $20 billion from roughly 1.2 million advertisers who believed they were bidding in standard second-price auctions. Amazon does not dispute the auction mechanics but argues cost-per-click stayed flat in real terms and that no advertiser ever pays more than their bid.

insights.claim: The FTC alleges Amazon has secretly and systematically overcharged approximately 1.2 million advertising customers since 2019 by overriding actual auction results with higher prices it sets itself, extracting over $20 billion.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: A $20 billion disgorgement claim against Amazon's fastest-growing high-margin segment is material enough to matter for ad-revenue quality assumptions.
insights.quote: Amazon’s scheme has likely illegally extracted over $20 billion from its unwitting advertising customers
insights.locator: The Federal Trade Commission and 22 states sued Amazon

insights.claim: Amazon has run generalized second-price auctions since 2012 but in 2019 began adding an undisclosed surcharge it internally calls a "soft reserve price," causing advertisers to pay more than the auction-determined price.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: The 2019 change is the damages start date; any settlement or restitution math anchors on seven years of surcharge revenue.
insights.locator: Amazon has run GSP auctions since 2012

insights.claim: The FTC quotes an Amazon senior scientist describing the mechanism as raising prices via "an invented auction participant representing how much Amazon thinks that particular ad slot is worth," and an Amazon senior VP for ads saying the second price "isn't set by an actual bidder" but by a proxy Amazon calculates.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Internal admissions in the operators' own words are the hardest evidence in deception cases and raise settlement probability.
insights.quote: an invented auction participant representing how much Amazon thinks that particular ad slot is worth
insights.locator: The FTC quoted an Amazon senior scientist

insights.claim: The lawsuit quotes a 2024 internal Amazon message reading "We don't tell them about the surcharge, we let them assume [it is] GSP-based," written by an employee who had helped run a large-scale pricing experiment concluding Amazon could increase surcharges without fear of detection by advertisers.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Documented intent plus a detectability experiment converts a pricing dispute into a deception case with punitive exposure.
insights.quote: We don’t tell them about the surcharge, we let them assume [it is] GSP-based
insights.locator: “We don’t tell them about the surcharge”

insights.claim: Amazon kept soft reserve prices secret even from its own sales and marketing employees who dealt with advertisers, designed the system to be undetectable by advertisers, and did not mention reserve pricing on its website until October 30, 2025 — almost a year after learning of the FTC investigation.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Disclosure timed to an investigation is read by regulators as consciousness of liability, weakening Amazon's good-faith defense.
insights.locator: Amazon kept the use of soft reserve prices secret

insights.claim: Amazon did not dispute key claims about the mechanics of its ad auctions but argued the system harmed neither consumers nor advertisers, saying the FTC cherry-picked a handful of simplified communications and educational videos out of approximately 1.5 million pages spanning six years.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Conceding mechanics and contesting only harm narrows the case to damages theory, which historically favors defendants in deception suits without price evidence.
insights.quote: the FTC cherry-picked a small number of materials

insights.claim: Amazon's core factual defense is that from 2019 through 2024 the average cost-per-click to advertisers remained flat when adjusted for inflation, so there were no price increases to pass on to consumers.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Flat real CPC is the single strongest data point Amazon has; if the FTC cannot rebut it, the consumer-harm leg of the case weakens considerably.
insights.quote: from 2019 through 2024, the average cost-per-click to advertisers remained flat when adjusted for inflation

insights.claim: Amazon says it uses both a hard reserve, the minimum bid needed to enter an auction that helps cover costs, and a soft reserve representing its estimate of the placement's true market value, and that in no scenario does an advertiser pay more than their bid.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: The two-reserve structure is a general pattern in ad exchanges; a ruling here would set expectations for reserve-price disclosure across the entire digital ad industry.
insights.quote: In no scenario does an advertiser pay more than their bid.
insights.locator: Amazon’s response acknowledged that it uses reserve prices

insights.claim: Amazon claims 92 percent of Sponsored Products ads do not go to the highest bidder because winners are selected on a combination of price and keyword relevancy, and that advertisers saved over $8 billion between 2021 and 2025 as a result of incorporating relevancy rather than bid alone.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Amazon is offsetting the alleged $20 billion extraction with an $8 billion claimed saving — expect the net-harm number to become the central contested figure.
insights.locator: Amazon also said 92 percent of Sponsored Products ads

insights.claim: The FTC and a bipartisan group of 22 state attorneys general, including Alaska, California, Florida, Idaho, New York and Washington, are seeking a permanent injunction plus civil penalties, restitution, disgorgement and other monetary relief in the US District Court for the Western District of Washington.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
entities: US District Court for the Western District of Washington
insights.so_what: Bipartisan state participation makes a quiet political resolution unlikely and raises the odds of a structural injunction on ad-pricing disclosure.
insights.locator: The FTC lawsuit was joined by a bipartisan group

insights.claim: For scale against the alleged $20 billion, Amazon reported $200.6 billion in net sales and $62.6 billion in net income in Q2 2026 alone.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: The claimed seven-year overcharge is smaller than a single quarter's net income, so financial impact is likely second-order to the injunctive remedy on ad-auction transparency.
insights.locator: The FTC and states are seeking a permanent injunction

insights.claim: The FTC argues that even after Amazon updated its website in April 2026 to note that reserve pricing may affect ad costs, it still fails to clearly and conspicuously disclose the nature, scope and extent of secret reserve pricing systems in place since 2018.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: The FTC is signaling that partial disclosure will not cure the claim, which points toward a prescriptive disclosure remedy rather than a wording fix.
insights.locator: FTC: Amazon still “fails to clearly” disclose system

insights.claim: The FTC frames inflated ad charges as compounding on account fees, referral fees, and fulfillment and storage fees that already cut into Amazon sellers' margins and lead to price increases borne by Amazon shoppers.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: The stacked-fee theory is the bridge from advertiser harm to consumer harm; if it holds it exposes Amazon's whole seller take-rate structure to scrutiny.
insights.locator: The FTC says customers paid more

top_entities: US District Court for the Western District of Washington
